Another option could be to reduce the number of tank transfers all together (e.g., drop-and-swap delivery method), thus reducing transfer losses. When LH is en route to the destination, the main source of losses is from heat transfer into the 2 tank causing the hydrogen to vaporize (boil-off). The vaporized hydrogen must eventually be vented to avoid unsafe pressure buildup in the storage tank. Typical boil-off losses during LH 2 trucking are similar to those for stationary LH storage tanks and are reported between 0.1% per 2 day and 5% per day (Frazer-Nash Consultancy 2022; Clean Energy Group 2025). In terms of advancements in liquid hydrogen tanker trucks to minimize boil-off, companies are exploring advanced insulation materials, active boil-off management systems, and advanced cryogenic storage states. Options for advanced insulation include using glass bubbles, aerogel blankets, and other concepts (Wijnans and Cardella, n.d.). The company 3MTM is a major producer of glass bubbles for insulation which have been shown to be a more effective insulation material than traditional materials (e.g., perlite) used to fill the annual space in cryogenic tanks (3MTM, n.d.; Wijnans and Cardella, n.d.). Active boil-off management systems work by recondensing boil-off gas in the storage tank or by keeping the hydrogen from boiling off to start. NASA has demonstrated this concept in its GODU-LH system and has integrated it into 2 LH storage tanks at Kennedy Space Center (Wijnans and Cardella, n.d.; Fesmire and Swanger 2 2021). This system uses a helium refrigerant and an internal heat exchanger to reduce boil-off gas formation. Companies such as GenH2 and Fabrum offer similar technologies with variations on the refrigeration approach (GenH2, n.d.-b; Fabrum 2024). Magnetic refrigeration is another promising boil-off mitigation pathway that requires further research and development before deployment (Wijnans and Cardella, n.d.). Transporting hydrogen in a supercritical cryo- compressed (40 K – 60 K, ~35 MPa) state or subcooled liquid (<20 K, 1.6 MPa) state are other methods to reduce boil-off. Hydrogen is more thermodynamically stable at these conditions compared to a liquid state at 20 K and atmospheric pressure. Cryo-compressed and subcooled hydrogen storage states are still at a R&D scale and are being considered for both onboard heavy-duty truck storage and H delivery applications (Pizzutilo et al. 2024; Lawrence 2 Livermore National Laboratory 2023). Another possible solution to eliminate boil-off during transport is to capture the boil-off and either use it directly on board the truck or store it for later use.
